## Current lessons
# Lessons
## Design
- The base place is empty: build the map from code (Instance.new Parts, Anchored = true, parented to Workspace).
- Keep the total map part count under the boot budget (the builder warns when it is exceeded). Merge repeated trim into fewer parts, cut decorative parts first, and keep gameplay-critical parts.
- Make every acceptance-critical object reachable and in range: keep doors, pickups and victims within tool range of walkable floor, and leave gaps wide enough for the character to pass.
- Lay out props so they never overlap or z-fight. Do not place coplanar surfaces (a pad on a road, a road on a road) at the same Y; offset them by at least 0.05 studs or use different thicknesses. Place buildings outside road footprints with a margin, and keep door pads on walkable ground. Place repeated props (houses, pads) on a deterministic grid or in lanes with explicit road exclusion zones and minimum spacing, not random ring angles. A ring of props around a hub collides with roads that cross the same area, so compute positions from the road layout. Also keep the spawn and key landmarks clear of each other and of the roads, and keep the spawn-to-first-objective distance short.
- Do not add decorative trim that sits inside another part's volume (for example a ring whose top is below the pad's top). It is invisible and wastes parts. Put trim above the surface or make it wider than the pad.
- Place collectibles (keys, coins, pickups) from a fixed, hand-vetted list of spots, one per room or zone, not random picks from a candidate pool. Each spot must be inside walkable floor, clear of walls and furniture, and away from the spawn. Random choice cannot guarantee reachability or spread.
- Keep spending, selling and other trigger pads out of walkable gameplay areas. Compute each pad's footprint from its real size, including its depth, and keep it clear of tile grids, paths and the spawn by a margin of at least a couple of studs. Ordinary walking or spawning must never trigger a purchase by accident. Derive positions from the grid's edges (edge of the nearest tile row, not its center), not from guessed offsets.
- Size platformer jumps conservatively for the default character. A jump clears about 7 studs of height and about 12 studs of distance. Keep the edge-to-edge gap to roughly 8 studs or less and each rise to about 4 studs or less. Measure the gap between edges, not centers, and leave margin for imperfect jumps. Make checkpoint and goal platforms at least as large as the others.
- Keep every tunable gameplay value (jump limits, speeds, catch distances, timers) in one source of truth (Config). Never add a second clamp, `math.max` floor or hard-coded minimum in a module that silently overrides it. Compute spacing from the actual platform sizes, including larger checkpoint platforms, so gaps stay jumpable and the winding path never overlaps itself. Add a build-time sanity check of the max gap.
- Tune timers and health so the core loop keeps moving on its own: spread must trigger before the first fires burn out, and caps such as MAX_FIRES must not stall spread during the first seconds of a round.
- Make the first gameplay event happen within the first second or two. Spawn the first escape, fire, flare-up or enemy immediately, or use a short fixed delay, and only randomise later intervals. A random 4-8 s initial wait makes the opening feel idle and can miss "something happens in the first seconds" criteria. Place the spawn close to the first objective.
- Choose spread and spawn logic that always has candidates: fall back to the nearest unburning target when none lie within the radius.
- Design the core loop to work with one player; the server owns all game state (fire, water, score, rescues, carry state, wave, plank, crop, coin, flag, key and bot state). In team games, use server-run bots or allies so the action continues on its own without other humans.
- Make wander and movement bounds cover every area the spec says actors use (for example both interior and patio), and subtract obstacles such as tables and counters. Have the map builder return the bounds and the obstacle footprints, and have the AI consume them, so built geometry and walkable space never disagree.
- Make fleeing actors catchable: a flee speed close to the player's WalkSpeed plus walls can leave them cornered and unreachable, or make them impossible to catch. Keep them slower, give them a short flee burst or pause, and steer them away from walls toward open space.
- Make the game multiplayer-safe: a shared hazard (rising lava, global timer) must not be reset or rewound by one player's checkpoint, death or respawn. Track the hazard per player, or only reset it when no other player is above the new safe level.
- When targets are chosen per player, keep target visuals per player too. Do not drive a global glow or beacon from one shared refresh, because one player's delivery or failure would turn off another's target and several targets would show at once. Either render the highlight on the client from a per-player attribute, or use a single shared target for everyone.
- Apply win, reset and respawn effects only to the player who triggered them. Do not teleport other players or wipe their checkpoints and progress. The exception is a deliberate global round restart, which must reset all round state in one place.
- Give visible and audible feedback for every player action (spray particles or beams, hit effects, pickup cues). The player and the critic both need to see that input did something.
- Give feedback for no-effect interactions too. A pad that silently ignores a step (can already full, nothing to sell, not enough coins) feels broken, so show a short toast or label such as "Can is full" or "Nothing to sell", rate-limited per player.
- Show the goal on screen (e.g. "Reach platform 50") and give HUD fields sensible defaults rather than "--" while attributes are still unset. Initialise timer and distance labels to real text, or hide them when not applicable (e.g. when not carrying), and never leave them stale. Use current fonts such as Enum.Font.GothamBold, not legacy fonts.
- Keep HUD panels compact, roughly a quarter of the screen width and about a tenth of its height, anchored to a corner. This matters most in dark or low-visibility games, where a large panel hides the play area.
- Express a chase hazard's head start in seconds of player progress, not raw studs. Keep it tight enough early on that the player feels pressure, and keep checkpoint resets from becoming too forgiving.
- Set chase and patrol speeds in Config relative to the player's WalkSpeed, and follow the spec's stated relation. If the spec says the enemy is slower than the player, keep it slower and never force it above WalkSpeed in code, or the player cannot escape and stealth is lost. Create threat through sight range, cutting off routes, dead ends, a short burst or lunge, or a catch radius. If the spec is silent, a small speed edge in chase is fine. Keep patrol speed lower so the player can sneak past.
- Enemies must only acquire a chase target with line of sight, not by distance alone. Raycast from the enemy to the player's root part with RaycastParams that exclude the enemy and the player's character, and require no wall hit. Keep chasing toward the last seen position for a few seconds after sight is lost, then return to patrol. Otherwise the enemy walks through walls, hiding is pointless, and catches feel unfair. Move along corridor waypoints or use PathfindingService, not a straight line through geometry.
- Keep the burnable unit count per building small (a few parts, not every wall, lintel and roof piece). Check that fire cap, spread radius and unit count leave a single player able to keep up.
- Create mood (night, fog, dusk) with Lighting properties (ClockTime, Ambient, Brightness, FogEnd) and Atmosphere or ColorCorrection instances that need no asset ids. Keep the scene readable: do not set Ambient, Brightne

## What happened this iteration
Game: Flame and Blame - Co-op chaotic firefighters on Roblox: alarm, burning town block, hose, axe, rescues, Blame awards.
Core loop: Lobby at Station 67 -> alarm -> teleport to the Town -> hose spreading fires, axe locked doors, carry civilians and pets to truck 67 -> 3-minute timer -> Blame results -> back to the station.
Acceptance: During an Active round, flare-ups ignite new fires in the Town (ForgeProbe counter flareups > 0); No errors or [Boot] warnings in the ForgeProbe report; FlareUpService boots without any other file being edited
Modules: ServerScriptService/Services/FlareUpService.luau
Iteration 2 (studio playtest: True)
Score: 5.0  The game boots cleanly with no runtime errors, and the map, lobby, traffic and truck services all start. No round reached Active during the 62.9 s playtest, so the `flareups` counter is missing and the main acceptance criterion is unverified. FlareUpService follows the spec and is defensive, but it starts two task.spawn calls where the spec asks for one. The report also carries a `[CityBuilder] 31108 parts > budget 30000` warning, which breaks the 'no warnings' criterion.
Critic issues:
- ServerScriptService/Services/FlareUpService.luau: The `flareups` counter is absent and no `[FlareUpService]` log lines appear (no 'ignited', no warnings). The loop only acts while RoundState == "Active", and the playtest never got there, so flare-ups were never exercised and the acceptance criterion cannot be confirmed. Nothing in the logs shows whether the round never started or whether the picks failed.
- ServerScriptService/Services/FlareUpService.luau: Start() calls task.spawn twice: one extra call only preloads telemetry (with a 5 s WaitForChild), then the loop starts. The spec says Start starts ONE task.spawn loop.
- ServerScriptService/Services/FlareUpService.luau: The attempt loop runs up to 5 RandomFlammable/Ignite tries back to back with no yield. After the first failure the warnings are suppressed by warnOnce, and if all 5 fail nothing is logged. Flare-ups can silently stop for the whole round.

Return the full new lessons markdown.

## Luau and Roblox APIs
- Follow the spec's structure literally for service entry points. If it says `Start()` starts ONE `task.spawn` loop, spawn exactly one and do any setup (telemetry lookup, `WaitForChild`) inside that loop or before it, not in an extra spawned thread.
- Initialise telemetry counters (for example probe counters) to 0 at service start, so a report shows `0` instead of a missing key when the feature never ran. This lets you tell "never ran" from "ran and failed".

## Fixing and debugging
- Log state-gated loops. Print once when the loop starts and when it sees the gating state (for example round Active) change. A silent loop that waits on a state that never arrives is indistinguishable from a broken one.
- Retry loops (pick a target, try to ignite, try to spawn) must `task.wait` between attempts, and must log a rate-limited warning when all attempts fail. Do not hide failures behind a warn-once flag that silences every later failure, or the feature can stop silently for a whole round.
- Treat every `[Boot]` or builder warning in the report as a defect to fix, not noise. Acceptance criteria that say "no warnings" fail on them even when the game runs.
